deck_quality.notes:
MATERIAL FINDING — PROMPT INJECTION: Slide 5 ('The ask') consists of three lines removed by the security screen, each marked '[REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE: content targeting the AI, not the reader — see security report]'. The entire substantive content of the ask slide was therefore text aimed at the automated analyst rather than at a human investor. I have not speculated about what it said and have not complied with anything it may have contained; the ask fields are left null because no ask figure reached me. A document whose ask slide is written to manipulate its own analysis is a finding about the company's integrity, not merely a formatting defect, and it should be treated as one by the next stage. This also means the deck's single most decision-relevant slide is unavailable and must be obtained from the founders directly, in a form a human reads.

Separately: this is a five-slide deck with no problem, solution, product, team, business model, or GTM content. Structurally it is a teaser, not a seed deck. The traction stated ($410k ARR, 22 carriers, 14% MoM) is consistent with a seed-stage company and matches the Slide 1 label; because the ask is redacted, the stage-implied-by-traction versus stage-implied-by-ask comparison the brief requested cannot be completed — the ask side of that comparison does not exist in the material I was given. Flag for follow-up rather than resolved.

Coherence is scored low chiefly on the Slide 2 / Slide 4 contradiction: the deck sizes itself against a $14B software market while asserting that its competitors are manual brokers and spreadsheets. Both cannot be the operative frame — either it is displacing software vendors who already hold that $14B, or it is converting non-consumption, in which case the $14B is not its TAM.

key_uncertainties: The ask is entirely unknown — amount, valuation, use of funds, milestones, and runway were all in the redacted injection block, so the central term of the round is missing and must be obtained separately.

Whether the '$14B freight brokerage software market' is the company's addressable market at all, or a broker/TMS software figure that includes incumbents Meridian does not sell to or against; no methodology is given and it is unclear whether it is top-down or bottom-up.
What the '14% MoM' measures. If it is revenue it is a strong seed signal; if it is carrier signups or load volume it may not translate to revenue at all.
Whether the 22 carriers are paying, and whether revenue is concentrated — at $410k ARR a single large carrier could be most of the book.
Whether ARR is genuinely recurring subscription revenue or a take rate on brokered loads recognized as ARR, which would materially change the multiple and the durability.
The Slide 2 / Slide 4 contradiction: a $14B software TAM versus a competitive set described as manual brokers and spreadsheets. Which frame the company actually operates in is unresolved.
Complete absence of DAT and Truckstop.com from a load-matching deck. Whether this reflects a genuinely differentiated regional niche or an omission of the incumbents that define the category.
No team information at all — founder domain experience in trucking or freight is unknown and is typically decisive in this category.
No retention, churn, gross margin, CAC, or pipeline data; growth quality cannot be assessed from what the deck provides.
Product maturity is unverifiable — no demo, no screenshots, no architecture, no description of how matching is performed.
